about.title: Hawaiian Gardens Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Hawaiian Gardens is a small, tightly packed city in Los Angeles County, home to warehouses, manufacturing shops, and small businesses along corridors like Carson Street and Norwalk Boulevard. Workers here face the same job-site hazards as anywhere else — falls, equipment failures, repetitive strain, and vehicle-related incidents on delivery routes. In California, workers' compensation is generally the only remedy against your own employer, no matter who was at fault. But when a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate claim against that third party may be possible alongside your workers' comp benefits. Because Hawaiian Gardens is a compact community with many small and mid-size employers, workplace injuries can involve multiple business owners, landlords, or contractors on a single site, which makes sorting out liability more complicated. LawProactive doesn't decide your case for you — we simply connect you with an independent attorney, at no cost, who can look at what happened and explain your options clearly.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About Your Workplace Injury

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: California treats workers' comp as the exclusive remedy against your employer in most cases, but a negligent third party — like a subcontractor or equipment maker — can still be held separately liable. An attorney can help identify whether a third-party claim applies to your situation.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer to preserve your workers' comp rights. Missing that window can complicate your claim, so getting guidance early matters.

items.title: Retaliation Protections Exist
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries or file claims. If you're worried about your job while dealing with an injury, an attorney can explain what protections apply to you.

items.question: I was hurt on a job site in Hawaiian Gardens that involved workers from more than one company. Does that change anything?
items.answer: It can. When multiple businesses or contractors share a work site, liability for an injury may extend beyond your direct employer to a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment supplier. An independent attorney can help figure out who else might be responsible alongside any workers' comp claim you file.

items.question: How long do I have to file a third-party injury claim in California?
items.answer: Third-party injury claims generally carry a two-year deadline from the date of the injury. This is separate from the 30-day window to report the injury to your employer for workers' comp purposes, so it's worth understanding both timelines.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for reporting an injury or filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: No, California law makes it illegal for employers to retaliate against workers for reporting an injury or pursuing a workers' comp claim. If you believe this happened to you, an attorney can review the details and explain your options.
